lesson.title: Jacob Riis and the Camera That Exposed the Slums
lesson.summary: Danish immigrant journalist Jacob Riis used pioneering flash photography and vivid reporting in his 1890 book How the Other Half Lives to expose the overcrowded, unsanitary tenement housing of New York City's poor, launching housing reform and helping set the template for muckraking journalism.
lesson.body:
Jacob Riis immigrated to the United States from Denmark in 1870 and spent years in poverty himself before becoming a police reporter in New York City, a job that took him nightly into the tenement districts of the Lower East Side. What he saw there, families of eight or ten crowded into a couple of dark, airless rooms, shared privies serving entire buildings, children sleeping in hallways and alleys, convinced him that most New Yorkers simply did not know how the other half of the city lived, and that if they saw it clearly they would demand change.

Riis's tool for making that case was as important as his argument. Existing photography could not capture interior scenes in the dark, cramped conditions of tenement housing, so Riis was among the first American journalists to adopt magnesium flash powder photography, which let him take pictures inside tenement rooms, opium dens, and police lodging houses at night. He combined these photographs with his own reporting into the 1890 book How the Other Half Lives: Studies Among the Tenements of New York, illustrated with woodcuts and halftone reproductions of his photographs, a format that hit readers with a visceral, documentary force that prose alone had not achieved.

The book landed years before the term muckraker existed and before the great wave of magazine exposes in the following decade, which is why Riis is often treated as an important precursor to the muckraking movement rather than a member of its main cohort. Its impact, however, matched anything the later muckrakers produced. Among the New Yorkers it reached was Theodore Roosevelt, then a rising political figure who would soon become the city's police commissioner. Roosevelt read the book, sought Riis out, and the two became allies and occasional companions on nighttime tours of the tenement districts, with Roosevelt using his official position to act on some of the conditions Riis had documented.

How the Other Half Lives helped build momentum for tenement housing reform in New York, contributing to the climate that produced the New York State Tenement House Act of 1901, which set stricter requirements for light, ventilation, and sanitation in new tenement construction. Riis's larger legacy lies in demonstrating that documentary evidence, especially photographic evidence, could move an issue like housing conditions from a problem the comfortable could ignore into one they could not, a lesson the muckrakers who followed him would apply to industries far beyond housing.
